papers.title: Bureaucratic Rigidity and Battle Outcomes: Evidence from Military Logistics in the Ming Dynasty
papers.abstract: Bureaucratic rules meant to improve accountability can undermine state effectiveness. We study a 1492 Ming dynasty reform that shifted military grain delivery from salt merchants to a state relay system with prefecture-to-prefecture handovers and fixed routes. Afterward, court records document more supply shortages at formerly merchant-supplied garrisons than at state-supplied ones. Using 406 defensive battles against foreign invaders, we find the reform reduced victory rates near these garrisons. Declines were largest where resupply mattered most (longer wars, walled-city defenses) and where the state’s rules were most costly (routes crossing more prefectures or exposed to floods, droughts, or rugged terrain).

papers.title: The Emergence of a National Capital Market,1870–1940
papers.abstract: This article documents the integration of the American capital market with the first long-run, geolocated, firm-level record of the asset holdings of large institutional investors: over 100,000 holdings of life insurers, 1870–1940. Between 1880 and 1890 the mean distance of insurers’ bonds from home more than doubled and their home-state share fell from over half to under a quarter. The shift occurred within firms, across bond classes and charters. Mortgage lending was national wherever state law permitted it. Integration was largely complete by 1890.
